task_row_model.query: In a hemodynamically stable adult with suspected pulmonary embolism and a moderate pretest probability, what is the recommended stepwise diagnostic algorithm? Please include how to apply D-dimer testing (including age-adjusted cutoffs) and how to choose between CTPA, V/Q scanning, or lower-limb ultrasound in patients with renal impairment, contrast allergy, or pregnancy.

documents.content: D-dimer assays are sensitive but nonspecific markers of fibrin degradation and are most useful to exclude venous thromboembolism in patients with low or intermediate clinical probability. Standard thresholds are assay-dependent; many centers use 500 ng/mL as the conventional cutoff. Older patients frequently have higher baseline D-dimer, leading to decreased specificity; age-adjusted strategies (for assays reported in ng/mL, commonly age × 10 for patients >50 years) improve specificity while maintaining sensitivity. Pretest probability must be assessed before ordering D-dimer; a positive result alone does not confirm PE and requires confirmatory imaging.

For patients with high-risk or massive pulmonary embolism, immediate management focuses on haemodynamic stabilization. Systemic thrombolysis is indicated for those with sustained hypotension or shock when benefits outweigh bleeding risk. Catheter-directed thrombolysis and surgical embolectomy are options when systemic therapy is contraindicated or ineffective. Close monitoring in an intensive care setting, consideration of vasopressors, and rapid imaging to confirm large obstructing thrombus are part of the emergent pathway. These treatment strategies assume the diagnosis has been established or is highly probable and address therapy rather than diagnostic sequencing.

Choice of imaging when PE is suspected depends on patient factors. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is first-line in many centers due to high sensitivity and wide availability. Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scanning is preferred when CTPA is contraindicated, such as severe contrast allergy or significant renal impairment; if the chest radiograph is normal, V/Q has high diagnostic yield. In pregnancy, a normal chest radiograph followed by V/Q may reduce fetal radiation; if chest radiograph is abnormal or V/Q unavailable, CTPA is acceptable. When imaging cannot be performed and suspicion is high, compression ultrasound of lower limbs can identify DVT and support anticoagulation decisions.

Recommended diagnostic approach for a hemodynamically stable adult: 1) Assess clinical probability using Wells or revised Geneva score. 2) If low or intermediate probability, obtain a D-dimer. Use age-adjusted cutoff for patients older than 50 (commonly age × 10 ng/mL when the assay uses a 500 ng/mL standard cutoff) to reduce false positives. 3) If D-dimer is below the threshold, PE is effectively excluded. 4) If D-dimer is positive or probability is high, proceed to imaging—CT pulmonary angiography is first-line in most settings. 5) If CTPA is contraindicated (contrast allergy or renal impairment) or unavailable, perform V/Q scanning; if V/Q is nondiagnostic and clinical suspicion remains, consider lower-extremity ultrasound or alternative imaging. 6) In pregnancy, consider compression ultrasound first if DVT symptoms present; otherwise use V/Q when chest radiograph is normal, with CTPA as an alternative if indicated.

Prevention of venous thromboembolism in hospitalized medical and surgical patients relies on risk stratification and appropriate prophylaxis. Mechanical methods such as intermittent pneumatic compression and graduated compression stockings are used when pharmacologic prophylaxis is contraindicated. Pharmacologic options include low molecular weight heparin, unfractionated heparin, or direct oral anticoagulants depending on surgical context and renal function. Duration of prophylaxis is individualized based on procedure, immobility, and ongoing risk factors. This material focuses on prophylactic strategies rather than diagnostic evaluation for suspected pulmonary embolism.
